notes.1a: This was not well known. Candidates were required to state that silver can form stable ions with incomplete d orbitals. A common error was stating silver has partially filled d-orbitals and forms stable ions.
notes.1b: (i) Most candidates gave the correct equation for the standard enthalpy change of atomisation of silver, including the correct state symbols. However, the enthalpy change of formation of silver fluoride was less well known and many candidates did not realise that one mole of silver fluoride was required as the product. Some candidates thought that silver fluoride was formed from its ions.
notes.1bii: This was generally well answered. Common errors were: • omitting ‘1 mole’ with ‘ionic compound formed’ • starting from 1 mole of gaseous ions.
notes.1iii: Candidates performed well on this question. Common errors included –308.5 (use of 79÷2), –269 (omission of 79) and –696 (use of 2 moles).
notes.1c: (i) Most candidates correctly calculated the enthalpy change of solution of AgF(s). A common error was –1925.
notes.1cii: Most candidates explained correctly that the negative H would make AgF soluble in water. sol Some candidates gained credit by error carried forward being applied to their answer from (c)(i).
notes.1d: (i) Many candidates could successfully explain the trend in electron affinities down Group 7. Some candidates referred to an increase in size of the ion rather than the atom. Many did not mention that the attraction of the nucleus for the incoming electron decreased as the size of the atom increased.
notes.1dii: Many gave an incomplete explanation for the decrease of the lattice energies from AgCl to AgI and did not mention that the attraction between ions become less when the halide ions become larger.
notes.1e: (i) The Eo value was calculated correctly by most candidates but the equation for the overall cell cell reaction was often constructed incorrectly.
notes.1eii: Of the three values to be inserted into the Nernst equation, most candidates were able to calculate the concentration of chloride ions in mol dm−3 (4.83). However, the Eo value for the silver electrode was often taken to be 0.12V, which was the value for the Eo and the number of electrons cell transferred, which should have been 1, was often given as 2.
notes.2a: (i) Many candidates did not understand that a large concentration of CH COCH was used to keep its 3 3 concentration constant so that it did not affect the rate. A common error was ‘to allow the reaction to go to completion’.
notes.2aii: Some very good answers were seen. On questions of this type candidates must ensure: • they identify the order with respect to the reactant that must be addressed first - in this case it was [H+] • they clearly identify which experiments each part of their explanation refers to • answers rely on explanation, not on annotations on the table.
notes.2iii: Some answers referred to constant half-life without presenting supporting evidence. It should be noted that ‘170 s and 330 s’ is not supporting evidence. ‘The time taken to halve from 100% to 50% is 170 s, the time taken to halve from 50% to 25% is 160 s’ is supporting evidence.
notes.2b: Many candidates identified mechanism 4 but found the explanation very difficult. Candidates were expected to explain that the rate equation given contained the species in the slow step of mechanism 4 in the correct stoichiometric amounts.
notes.2cii: Most candidates were able to calculate the correct pH of solution. A common error was pH = 1.98 (error carried forward from [H+] = 0.010592)
notes.2d: (i) Most candidates knew the definition in the syllabus. Some did not give a precise definition, stating that the pH would remain unchanged or omitted ‘small’ amounts of acid and base should be added.
notes.2dii: This proved difficult for many candidates. In particular, the number of moles of acid C left. Common errors included 3.55 (0.05 used instead of 0.03) and 4.13 (reverse ratio used 0.03÷0.02).
notes.3a: (i) Most candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.3aii: Many successfully completed all the boxes in Table 3.1 with information about the different Fe2+ and Fe3+ complexes. Two common errors were writing Cl or Cl as the ligand in [FeCl ]2− and 2 4 giving the coordination number of 3 for [Fe(en) ]3+.
notes.3b: (i) Most candidates gave good explanations of the differences in colour.
notes.3bii: This proved challenging to most candidates. Many gave an expression with charges outside the last set of brackets. Some others were written the wrong way up, or with [H O] included in the expression.
notes.3iv: Many candidates were able to state that the solution turned from purple to colourless, but some candidates thought the solution would then turn red on addition of the KSCN. Some unusual answers were seen, for example precipitates being formed and the use of ‘common ion effect’, in the explanation.
notes.3c: (i) Better performing candidates were able to write balanced half-equations for both the oxidation of C O 2− and the reduction of MnO −. However, many found working out the half-equations 2 4 4 challenging and H+ was often seen as a reactant in the oxidation of C O 2−. Candidates need to be 2 4 reminded that they should balance the charges as well as the species in the half-equations.
notes.3cii: Many completely correct calculations were seen, but others found the calculation very difficult, only gaining one or two marks. Nearly all candidates were able to work out the amount of the manganate(VII) ion and but did not always multiply this by the correct ratio of 5÷2 to obtain the moles of ethanedioate ion.
notes.4a: Most candidates gave the correct order of basicity. The positive inductive effect of the propyl group was well known for propylamine being the strongest base. However, many did not link basicity to the availability of the lone pair on the nitrogen atom to accept a proton. The ability of the lone pair on the nitrogen to attract a proton is not sufficient. Only higher performing candidates were able to explain the delocalisation of the lone pair on nitrogen into the C=O group in propanamide.
notes.4b: This was answered well by many candidates. L and M were more well known than K. Common errors included: • for K: CH CH COOH 3 2 • for M: Sn and conc. HCl or NaBH .
notes.4c: Many candidates were able to draw the hydrolysis products benzylamine and ethanoic acid but did not realise that benzylamine would be protonated in excess concentrated hydrochloric acid. The third hydrolysis product proved much more challenging. A common error were structures containing an acyl chloride instead of a carboxylic acid group.
notes.4d: (i) This question discriminated well. Some unbalanced equations were seen without H O in the products. Other common errors were use of [H+] (instead of [H]) or forming O as a by-product.
notes.4dii: Many incorrect reagents and conditions were seen. The types of reaction were well known, although oxidation was a common error for step 2. Some candidates who chose to name the reagent in step 4 (instead of the formula (CH ) CHCH CH OH) often gave the incorrect name, 3 2 2 2 3-methylbutanol, instead of 3-methylbutan-1-ol.
notes.5a: Most candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.5iii: Many candidates knew the structure for the benzene diazonium ion, however placed the positive charge on the wrong nitrogen.
notes.5iv: This was answered well by many candidates. Diazo and diazonium group were common incorrect answers.
notes.5c: (i) The standard entropy change of reaction 1 was correctly calculated by the majority of candidates.
notes.5cii: The correct use of the Gibbs free energy equation was required to show that reaction 1 was feasible. Some candidates did not correctly convert 25°C to 298 K.
notes.5d: (i) The condition required for the reaction of bromine with phenol was for the bromine to be aqueous. Some candidates just described the condition as room temperature which was insufficient. Many correctly stated that the lone pair on oxygen was delocalised into the ring, although omitted to explain that this increased its electron density. The final part of the explanation was omitted by many candidates, that the increased electron density in the ring polarised the bromine molecule more.
notes.5dii: Most candidates drew 2,4,6-tribromophenol. Some incorrectly gave the mono-brominated phenol.
notes.5v: The two isomers of dinitrophenol were usually drawn correctly. The explanation for the nitro groups being in the 2, 4 positions was less well known. Most stated that the ─OH group was electron donating but did not state that it was 2, 4-directing.
notes.6a: (i) The ester group was usually drawn correctly but the rest of the molecule was found to be more challenging. Common errors included: • drawing more than one repeat unit and • omitting some hydrogen atoms in their structure.
notes.6aii: Although KMnO was usually identified as the suitable reagent, sometimes one of the three conditions of cold, acidified and dilute was omitted in their answer.
notes.6b: (i) Most candidates gave the correct answer.
notes.6bii: This was answered correctly by the majority of candidates.
notes.6iii: There were some very good answers seen. Candidates needed to carefully consider all the information given in 6(c) to draw a correct structure of X. They were told X was an aromatic compound and there was a positive triiodomethane test. This suggested CH CO─ bonded to the benzene ring. The loss of the two NMR signals in D O solvent suggested there were also two ─OH groups attached to the ring. These were in unsymmetrical positions around the benzene ring because this was the only way to produce eight different carbon environments. Some of the carbon-13 spectrum signals confirmed these conclusions, for example the peak at 205 for a carbonyl carbon and at 62 for a carbon next to a C=O.
notes.6c: (i) Many candidates gave the correct number of eight carbon environments but four and six were common incorrect answers.
notes.6cii: Many candidates understood that dissolving X in D O would remove OH peaks.
notes.key_messages:
• Candidates must ensure their presentation is clear.
• Chemical equations, ionic equations and half-equations should always be balanced for substances and
• In organic reaction mechanisms, the starting and finishing points of curly arrows are a key part in the
description of the mechanisms. Curly arrows should always start in a precise place and should be
pointing towards a precise place.
notes.general_comments:
The correct convention is needed when writing the formulae of substances. For example, potassium
manganate(VII) should be written KMnO and not KmNO4 or KMNO .
